subject: maths

moments.title: Euclid's Elements
moments.body:
Euclid, working at the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy I, compiles the Elements: 13 books deriving plane geometry, number theory and solid geometry from 5 axioms (postulates) and 5 common notions. Every later proposition builds rigorously on what came before.

The Elements is one of the most translated, printed and studied books in history. It is the standard geometry textbook for over 2000 years.
moments.takeaway: The Elements is the founding document of axiomatic mathematics. Everything follows from explicit rules.

moments.title: The parallel postulate problem
moments.who: Multiple — Ptolemy, Proclus, Wallis, Saccheri, Lambert
moments.body:
Euclid's fifth postulate (the parallel postulate) is messier than the others: 'If a line crosses two others such that the interior angles on one side sum to less than 180°, those two lines meet on that side.'

Mathematicians for 2000 years try to prove the parallel postulate from the other four. They cannot. Many produce 'proofs' that turn out to assume what they were trying to prove.
moments.takeaway: The parallel postulate resists every attempt at proof. The community keeps trying.

moments.title: Non-Euclidean geometry
moments.body:
Janos Bolyai (Hungarian) and Nikolai Lobachevsky (Russian) independently realise: the parallel postulate cannot be proved because it's INDEPENDENT. You can replace it with a different postulate and get a consistent geometry.

Bolyai's father sends his son's manuscript to Carl Friedrich Gauss, who replies that he had worked it out himself decades earlier but had not published for fear of controversy. Bolyai is devastated.

Riemann (1854) generalises further: any 'curved' space can be geometry. Spherical geometry, hyperbolic geometry, and Euclidean geometry are special cases of Riemannian geometries.
moments.takeaway: Euclidean geometry is just one of many possible geometries. Reality is not necessarily Euclidean.

moments.title: General relativity uses Riemannian geometry
moments.body:
Einstein, helped by mathematician Marcel Grossmann, uses Riemannian geometry to describe gravity. Spacetime curvature replaces gravitational force. The Schwarzschild solution (1916) for a spherically symmetric mass gives a non-Euclidean geometry around stars and planets.

The non-Euclidean geometry that mathematicians invented as abstract speculation turns out to describe the actual universe.
moments.takeaway: Pure mathematics, developed for its own sake, becomes the foundation of fundamental physics.

moments.title: Hilbert reorganises foundations
moments.body:
Hilbert publishes 'Grundlagen der Geometrie' (Foundations of Geometry), giving a fully rigorous axiomatic basis for Euclidean geometry. He adds axioms that Euclid had used without stating (e.g., axioms about order on a line).

Hilbert's broader program: every branch of mathematics should be built from explicit axioms. Gödel later showed this couldn't be completed for arithmetic — but for geometry, Hilbert succeeded.
moments.takeaway: Modern mathematics is axiomatic. Geometry was the prototype, and Hilbert finished the job Euclid started.

now.title: Geometry today
now.body:
We have spherical, hyperbolic and many other geometries. Differential geometry handles curvature on manifolds of any dimension. Topology cares about connectivity ignoring distance. Algebraic geometry treats geometric objects via their defining equations.

Geometry shows up in physics (general relativity, gauge theories), computer graphics, robotics, GPS, neural network architectures (manifold learning), and pure abstraction.
now.open_questions: What's the shape of the universe? (CMB measurements show it's spatially flat to within measurement error, but we don't know if it's finite or infinite.) Can we visualise 4D geometry effectively? Are mathematical structures (categories, spaces) somehow 'more real' than physical reality?

reflection: Gauss did the non-Euclidean work himself but didn't publish because he feared 'the clamor of the Boeotians'. Bolyai's father wrote to him about his son's work; Gauss replied saying he already knew it. Bolyai stopped publishing in despair. What does it tell us about science that a great mathematician's caution effectively suppressed his own discovery — and how should the discipline treat people whose contributions were de-prioritised?
